blocks.content: The 7:40 bus stopped at the curb two buildings before The Copper Mug.

I know its sound by now — the hydraulic exhale when it slows, the particular way the doors open. I don't usually look. I know the people who get off. The same ones, most mornings, doing the same thing.

She was the last one off. Red hair, paper cup, a silver bracelet that caught the morning light for just a second before she turned. She had a stuffed dinosaur tucked under one arm — purple, worn at the corners — the way you carry something you stopped thinking about a long time ago.
She laughed at something on her phone. Not a polite laugh. The real kind, the kind that happens before you can decide whether to let it.

I crouched and retied it anyway. I needed somewhere for my eyes to go and the sidewalk was the least complicated option. I took my time. When I stood up she was already crossing the street, still laughing, the dinosaur still under her arm.
I stood there for a moment.
Then I pushed open the door of The Copper Mug and went inside.
